title: OpenAI says a research run produced 948 local paths to root in Linux
friendlyTitle: OpenAI says a research run found 948 ways for a normal Linux user to become root
summary: On 4 November, OpenAI said a research pipeline, run in a controlled environment in mid-October, started from 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, reproduced 1,724, and produced 948 working local privilege-escalation exploits plus 291 information-leak proofs. The run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, about $1,279 per privilege-escalation exploit. People reviewed the output before reports went to maintainers. OpenAI says it began with critical cases and is working with Linux kernel partners through Patch the Planet. It also says the newer model found more than five times as many novel local privilege escalations as a GPT-5.6 Sol run in July, after three months of hardening in between. It does not say those patches are already in a distribution you can install.
friendlySummary: On 4 November, OpenAI said a research system, run in a controlled lab in mid-October, started with 2,308 possible Linux kernel problems, reproduced 1,724 of them, and built 948 working cases where a normal local user could become the administrator. It also built 291 proofs of information leaks. The run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, about $1,279 for each administrator-level case. People checked the results before they were sent to the kernel maintainers. OpenAI says it started with the most serious cases and is working with Linux partners through a project it calls Patch the Planet. It also says the newer model found more than five times as many new administrator-level cases as a GPT-5.6 Sol run in July, even after three months of fixes in between. It does not say those fixes are already in the Linux version you can install.
whyItMatters: OpenAI's own practical line is the one to keep: a low-privilege account on an operating system that is behind on patches should be treated, for a well-resourced attacker, as close to full control. Update the kernel. A sandbox still limits the damage of a bug that is known and not yet installed. A research count is not a patch list, and it is not a reason to go looking for the bugs yourself.
